lesson.title: Stop and Wait: The One Frame at a Time Baseline
lesson.summary: Stop and wait ARQ is the simplest reliable transfer protocol: the sender transmits exactly one frame, then blocks until it receives an acknowledgment or its timer expires, trading throughput for the simplest possible bookkeeping.
lesson.body:
Stop and wait is automatic repeat request stripped down to its minimum viable form. The sender is allowed exactly one outstanding, unacknowledged frame at any moment. It sends frame 0, starts a timer, and then does nothing else, no new data leaves the sender, until either an acknowledgment for frame 0 arrives or the timer expires. Only then does it move on: either to retransmit frame 0 on timeout, or to send frame 1 once the acknowledgment is received. This is why a single alternating bit, 0 then 1 then 0 again, is enough sequence number space. Since only one frame is ever in flight, there is never ambiguity about which frame an acknowledgment refers to.

The protocol has to handle three distinct failure modes, and it is worth tracing each one. If the data frame is lost or corrupted in transit, the receiver never gets anything to acknowledge, the sender's timer expires, and it retransmits the same frame with the same sequence number. If the data frame arrives safely but the acknowledgment is lost on the way back, the sender still times out, since it has no way to know the frame actually arrived, and retransmits. The receiver, seeing a duplicate sequence number, discards the duplicate data but resends the acknowledgment so the sender can finally advance. If the acknowledgment is merely delayed rather than lost, the sender may retransmit unnecessarily, but the sequence number still lets the receiver detect and drop the duplicate cleanly.

Concretely: the sender transmits frame 0 with data D0. It arrives, and the receiver sends ACK0. That ACK0 is lost. The sender's timer for frame 0 expires, so it retransmits frame 0, still carrying D0 with the same sequence number 0. The receiver sees sequence number 0 again, recognizes it as a duplicate of data it already delivered upward, discards the payload, but sends ACK0 again. This second ACK0 reaches the sender, which now sends frame 1 with data D1. The receiver's reliance on the sequence number, not the content, is what prevents D0 from being delivered twice to the application.

The obvious cost is throughput. If a frame takes time Tf to transmit and the round trip time is RTT, the sender spends Tf transmitting but then sits idle for roughly RTT waiting on the acknowledgment before it can send again. On a high bandwidth, high delay path, such as a satellite link, Tf can be a tiny fraction of RTT, so the link sits idle almost the entire time and effective throughput collapses far below the link's raw capacity. This inefficiency is precisely the motivation for sliding window protocols, which let the sender keep several frames outstanding at once instead of stalling after every one.

Stop and wait is rarely used by itself in modern high speed networks for exactly that reason, but it remains the clearest way to see the core ARQ machinery, timers, sequence numbers, and acknowledgments, working together. It is still a reasonable choice on links where simplicity matters more than throughput, such as some low power sensor networks or very short, low latency hops where RTT is negligible next to Tf.
